extracted.intended_audience: government contracting officers, procurement lawyers, contractors and judges/practitioners interpreting government contracts
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of legal holdings and interpretive rules governing United States government contracts (Army/War Department context): scope, performance, approvals, bidders' obligations, risk allocation, remedies, and regulatory applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No obligation to give surety opportunity absent contract/bond provision
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a provision in the contract or accompanying bond requiring the Government to call upon the surety to carry out the contract in the case of a default of the contractor, the Government would be under no obligation to give the surety such an opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding C. 24639, Mar. 27, 1909 — if the contract/bond lacks a clause obligating the Government to require surety performance, the Government may proceed without offering the surety an opportunity to perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing partner to take up dissolved partnership's bid is equivalent to rejecting and rebidding
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the lowest bidder was a partnership and before the contract could be signed the partnership was dissolved, there is no legal objection to allowing one of the members to take up the bid and enter into a contract; this is equivalent to rejecting all bids and making a contract without further advertisement with that partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 12827, Sept. 10, 1902 — contracting with a former partner after dissolution stands as a post-bid open-market transaction, treated like a new award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments to partners may be made to any member despite protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments due on a contract where the contractors are partners may legally be made to any member of the firm, notwithstanding one of them may have filed a protest and notice against payment to one of the partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 3210, May 20, 1897 — Government payment to a firm member binds the partnership despite internal protests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army Regulations not strictly binding on Soldiers' Home when board authorized to set rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations are not strictly applicable to contracts of the United States Soldiers' Home, as the home is under the control of a board of commissioners expressly empowered to establish its own regulations; however, Army Regulations may be followed where the board has not prescribed different regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19921, June 16, 1906 — where a distinct statutory governance exists, apply local board rules first; Army regs serve as persuasive guidance unless superseded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee contract provision requiring notice and forfeiture not unreasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed contract requiring an employee not to leave the Engineer Department without consent of the local representative and to give 50 days' notice, with forfeiture of pay upon violation, was held not unreasonable or oppressive and had no legal objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23026, Apr. 3, 1908 — restraints in employment contracts and forfeiture clauses can be upheld if not oppressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inviting bids does not abandon government's renewal option
rubrics_metrics.description: Government advertising for bids for a new term does not constitute abandonment of a contractual option to renew; it is a means of ascertaining whether it will be in the Government's interest to exercise the option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 28614, June 10, 1911 — soliciting competing bids while holding an option does not waive the option unless clear intent to abandon is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract scope: specific activities (e.g., quartermaster printing) may be excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract for printing to serve Headquarters Atlantic Division and Department of the East during the fiscal year did not include printing for a constructing quartermaster carrying on construction under the Quartermaster General — i.e., certain operational printing functions were outside the contract scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23212, July 7, 1908 — interpret contract language against expansive inclusion of unrelated operational tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statute requires War Department contracts to be under seal
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statute that requires contracts under the War Department to be under seal; therefore a corporation contracting with the War Department need not attach its corporate seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 2878, Jan. 19, 1897 — formalities such as a corporate seal are not mandatory absent statutory requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval condition: contract not binding until required superior approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract expressly provided that it 'shall be subject to approval of the Chief of Engineers,' the contract was duly signed but not approved before contractor failed; the Chief could legally refuse to approve the contract or could approve it and permit a receiver to carry it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 7508, Jan. 6, 1900 — a contract conditioned on supervisory approval is not a binding subsisting agreement until that approval is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervising officers may withhold approval for obsolete or unsuitable items
rubrics_metrics.description: Where bids were requested for a type of pickaxe considered obsolete and the contract was subject to approval of the Quartermaster General, he could properly withhold approval and call for bids for a more suitable kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 28136, Apr. 14, 1911 — approving authorities may refuse approval when the item is unsuitable or obsolete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of force majeure terms (‘force or violence of the elements’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract language allowing time extensions for 'freshets, ice, or other force or violence of the elements' should be construed to mean forces like those specified; a loss (e.g., dredge lost by fire not from lightning) may not qualify; contractor must show inability to replace the dredge to claim excusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 12598, May 18, 1908 — general words following specific instances are limited to similar cases; mere non-negligent loss does not automatically excuse performance absent inability to mitigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary extra work without order is nonrecoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the contractor removed large bowlders not required under the contract and without contract, order, or request from the proper officer, such extra work was voluntary and no recovery against the Government could be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 63, 180, Jan. 10, 1894; C. 23546, Nov. 3, 1910 — contractors should obtain orders/authority before performing extra work to secure recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract provision allowing price increase to cover collectible duty
rubrics_metrics.description: An invitation that proposals will be considered with free entry of materials, with proviso that if duty is collectible the contract price will be increased to cover the duty, later made part of the contract; when contractor paid duty he could request additional payment and there was no legal objection to making such payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 24076, Dec. 30, 1908 — explicit contract clauses allocating duty risk are enforceable and can justify contract price adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply delivery obligations limited to service needs at contract location
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract for delivery of forage 'at the various stables, officers' quarters, and other places in the city of Washington and within one mile beyond the limits of said city' was interpreted to supply forage required to meet needs of the service at Washington and immediate vicinity; not to permit Quartermaster to require furnishing beyond those needs for shipment elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 29239, Nov. 14, 1911 — delivery clauses are construed according to the service needs and geographic scope specified; don't expand to supply distant posts absent explicit terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase 'for heirs, executors, and administrators' not essential to enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression in a contract that the contractor 'agrees for -7 heirs, executors, and administrators' is not essential; personal representatives of a deceased contractor may carry out his contracts and the estate is liable for debts independently of that phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 2878, Jan. 19, 1897 — wills/estate liability uphold contractual obligations despite omission of survivorship language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality standard 'best merchantable quality... of locality' as receiving-officer benchmark
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract language that forage 'be of the best merchantable quality and of the highest recognized commercial grade of the locality' supplies a standard by which the receiving officer judges quality; 'locality' refers to sources from which the forage could reasonably be obtained for the post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 1993, Jan. 22, 1896; 2673, Oct. 12, 1896 — interpret qualitative terms as objective standards tied to reasonable local commercial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidders bear risk where specs state conditions not guaranteed and advise to satisfy themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Where specifications state the character of material is not guaranteed and bidders are expected to satisfy themselves, encountering unexpectedly difficult material does not entitle contractor to additional compensation; original contract terms govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 13625, Oct. 23, 1902; C. 17234, Dec. 16, 1904; C. 20875, Jan. 7, 1907 — if specs warn bidders to ascertain conditions, the contractor assumes the risk of unexpected conditions absent express guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor bound to perform to specifications regardless of encountered material
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contract requires delivery of complete and finished construction and bidders were warned to ascertain material nature, the contractor is bound to construct in conformity with the specifications even if unforeseen materials (e.g., quicksand pockets) make performance difficult; supplemental contracts to pay higher prices cannot legally be made if not for Government benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 5082, Oct. 10, 1898; Simpson v. U.S., 172 U.S. 372 — contractors assume construction risk and mutual mistake is not grounds to reform the contract absent extraordinary circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express statement about river bed not a conclusive government guarantee where other provisions put bidders on notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause stating 'the river bed at No. 2 consists of gravel throughout' did not constitute a guaranty by the United States where other contract provisions advised bidders to visit site and ascertain conditions; unit-based pricing means site differences affect cost to the United States, not the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 524, Nov. 6, 1898 — reconcile isolated descriptive language with surrounding 'inspect and satisfy yourself' clauses; bidders charged with inspecting differing sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may undertake construction and make reciprocal agreements for benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: When an extension of sewer was necessary to protect a post water supply and the sewer will be Government property, the Secretary of War may properly authorize its construction as a Government undertaking and may legally authorize agreement with the water company to reduce price of water as consideration until the saving equals the cost of extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 26930, Dec. 8, 1910 — Government may authorize projects and related contractual accommodations when legally justified as incidents of public works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery time measured from contract date unless contract specifies otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: Where bidding instructions asked bidders to state days from date of award and bidder's offer referenced 'from acceptance of bid', but the written contract specified delivery 'from the date of contract' and was dated earlier than approval, supplies were to be delivered within the number of days after the contract date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 26752, May 23, 1910 — follow the express time-reference in the executed contract (contract date) rather than subjective bidder expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government's election to order minimum quantity can terminate contract; damages measured accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: In a cement contract with option to increase/decrease by 50% (min 5,000 of 10,000), when cement failed tests and the Government elected to order only the minimum and notified no further orders would be made, the contract was terminated; Government entitled to recover contractor's loss only on the minimum quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 26155, May 9, 1910 — exercise of contractual option by Government can effect termination and limit measure of damages to the quantity effectively ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: General procurement regulation applies to all military personnel including retired officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 525, Army Regulations, requiring that information regarding supplies/services for which proposals are invited be furnished to all persons on application, but forbidding persons in military service from rendering assistance in preparation of proposals, is general and includes all persons belonging to the military service, including retired officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 16166, Nov. 15, 1905 — regulatory restrictions on assisting bidders apply broadly to military-affiliated persons unless exception stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation about settlement with heirs applies only to accounts arising from dealings with decedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 734, Army Regulations, providing disbursing officers will not settle with heirs/executors/administrators except by authority and upon audited accounts, refers only to accounts arising out of dealings with the testator/intestate and does not refer to contracts made with an executor or administrator in his official capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 16550, July 6, 1904 — interpret settlement restrictions in light of origin of the account (personal estate vs. official contractual dealings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War may require proposed open-market purchases be submitted for approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute limiting open-market purchases (aggregate amount not to exceed $200) and requiring reporting to the Secretary of War vests the Secretary with power to make regulations and legally require proposed open-market purchases to be submitted for his approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 1112, Mar. 12, 1895 — administrative oversight of procurement is within Secretary's power to carry legislation into effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts should not call for payment in foreign coin where statute restricts disbursing officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3651, R.S., forbids disbursing officers to exchange funds furnished them except certain exceptions; thus a Government contract should not call for payment in foreign coin, though contract terms specifying U.S. money equivalent to foreign coin at a bank would not conflict with the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 8393, July 9, 1900 — prefer specifying payment in recognized U.S. currency forms to avoid conflicts with disbursing statutes; equivalency clauses may be acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial practice accepts typewritten/rubber-stamp firm signatures except for formal instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications and papers received from business firms with the firm name signed by typewriter or rubber stamp should be accepted in view of commercial practice, except as to formal instruments such as formal vouchers, contracts, bonds, bids, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 27933, Mar. 3, 1911 — for informal commercial correspondence accept mechanical signatures; for formal, require proper executed signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervising official may set or change contractual tests and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract providing a test to be prescribed by the Secretary allowed the Secretary, after initially apparently approving a contractor suggestion, to set aside that approval and prescribe whatever test of endurance he might decide appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 6945, Aug. 28, 1899 — when contract delegates specification of tests/standards to a supervising official, that official has discretion to define or change the tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to include work in periodic sworn statements not bar to payment if work performed and covered by contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract required daily sworn itemized statements and after completion bills for amounts not included in the daily statements were submitted, if the work represented by the bills was actually performed and covered by the contract the United States is legally bound to pay notwithstanding failure to include it in the daily statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 10299, May 4, 1901 — formal reporting requirements do not automatically preclude payment for contract work actually performed and proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner's implied authority doesn't extend to sealed instruments without express authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied authority of a partner to execute contracts for the firm does not extend to contracts under seal; a bill of sale under seal signed by only one partner needs evidence of express authority from the other partners, though a contemporaneous statement by the other partners plus delivery and payment may pass title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 4611, July 18, 1898 — obtain express authority or confirmatory statements when sealed instruments are executed by a single partner to ensure clear title transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of nonconforming goods may be conditioned on substitute security/bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an installed cylinder did not meet contract tests but was likely satisfactory, it was permissible to accept it upon the contractor filing a surety bond conditioned to replace the cylinder and pay for hire of substitutes if replacement proved necessary within two years, and an additional bond from the contractor to cover remaining period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 26577, Apr. 22, 1910 — contracting officers may accept substandard performance with remedial security (bonds) protecting Government interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidder entitled to use officers of his choosing to execute contract papers (subject to Government requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When bidder was directed to appear at an office to execute contract and bring sureties, he has a right to go before officers of his own choosing (if they meet Government requirements) to execute bond and affidavits; Government cannot require appearance before a particular official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 167, Aug. 18, 1894 — contractors may complete formalities before suitable officials of their choice; contracting officers may accept validly executed documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include clauses for international transit: permissions, duties, and political-risk loss allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: For transport through foreign territory: (a) troops — insert clause requiring carrier to obtain written consent of foreign government and require alternative routing if refused; (b) supplies — include clause requiring contractor to pay any duties or impositions so they do not become a charge against the United States; (c) where conditions unsettled, include clause requiring carrier to make good loss from political disturbances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 14552, Dec. 18, 1903; C. 28430, May 26, 1911 — anticipate international law and local impositions; explicitly allocate customs, permission, and political-risk responsibilities to contractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor not liable for ordinary damages from contemplated methods performed with reasonable care
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasting carried on in execution of a contract injured plastering; blasting was carried on with reasonable care; in absence of facts showing blasting performance was not contemplated or that contractor assumed responsibility for damages, no recovery could be had against the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 27673, Jan. 23, 1911 — if method of performance (e.g., blasting) is reasonably necessary and performed carefully, Government cannot recover for incidental damages unless contractor assumed liability or method was outside contemplated performance.
